(CNN) — Pakistan’s former president said his country was being treated “unequally” compared with other nations, despite being a staunch U.S. ally in the war on terror.

Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf said anti-American sentiment in Pakistan was high.

“Pakistan is being treated so unequally, while we are the ones who are in the lead role fighting the global war on terror,” Musharraf said in an interview with CNN’s Wolf Blitzer for “The Situation Room.”

“This is what hurts Pakistan. It hurts the leadership. Indeed, it hurts the government. It hurts the people of Pakistan,” said Musharraf, speaking from Dallas, Texas, during a U.S. book tour.

The interview took place amid reports Friday that U.S. drones had struck militant targets in Pakistan, just days after the start of the Obama administration, which had made combating al Qaeda and Taliban militants in Pakistan’s tribal region near Afghanistan its most immediate national security priority.

Asked whether he was comfortable with the attacks continuing under a new U.S. president, Musharraf replied: “Nobody in Pakistan is comfortable with the strikes across the border. There is no doubt in that. Public opinion is very much against it.

“But as far as this issue of the new president—President Obama having taken over and this continuing—I have always been saying that policies don’t change with personalities; policies have national interest, and policies depend on an environment.

“So, the environment and national interest of the United States being the same, I thought policies would remain constant,” he said.

Watch Musharraf address the reported U.S. airstrike »

Musharraf also addressed his statement that the $10 billion in assistance Pakistan had received from the United States was a “pittance for a country which is in the lead role to fight terrorism.”

He emphasized his gratitude to the United States for the funding but said the amount was small compared with the billions spent in Afghanistan and “maybe over a trillion dollars” in Iraq.

“Please don’t think that this $10 billion was such a great amount that we ought to be eternally grateful, while we know that we deserve much more, and we should have got much more, and we must get much more if we are to fight the global war on terror,” he said.

Musharraf stressed that Pakistan had been “in the lead role fighting a war for you for 10 years, between ’79 and ’89,” referring to Pakistan’s alliance with the United States and the Afghan mujahedeen rebels during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.

He emphasized that, for 42 years leading up to 1989, Pakistan had been a “strategic partner” of the United States. However, many Pakistanis felt abandoned by the United States after the Russians withdrew from Afghanistan.

Musharraf said the 1989 “peace dividend” went to Europe—Eastern Europe. Pakistan was “left alone” from 1989 to 2001, and during that period, the militant Taliban movement took control of Afghanistan.

“What did Pakistan get out of fighting for 10 years with you? Nothing, sir,” he said, explaining why public opinion in Pakistan had become “so much against the United States.”

Musharraf said public opinion in his country was strongly opposed to U.S. drone strikes against militants in Pakistan’s tribal region. Although al Qaeda and the Taliban must be confronted, he said, “public opinion is certainly against the methodology being adopted.”

Watch Musharraf say Pakistan is not sponsoring terrorism »

Musharraf, a former Pakistani army chief, resigned under intense political pressure in August as the ruling coalition began taking steps to impeach him. He had swept to power in 1999 in a bloodless coup.

Asked why al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, who was believed to be somewhere in the border region, had not been found, Musharraf replied:

“I would like to ask the United States why he hasn’t been found. They have their intelligence. You have more intelligence capability. I would like to ask the United States why Mullah Omar has not been found, who is the leader of all of the Taliban in Afghanistan.”

(CNN) — Pervez Musharraf, Pakistan’s former president, accused the United States of applying a double standard to his country even though Pakistan has been a committed partner in the campaign against terrorism. He also said anti-U.S. feeling among Pakistanis remains widespread.

Speaking from Dallas, Texas, while touring the United States to promote a book, Musharraf discussed the issue with CNN’s Wolf Blitzer on “The Situation Room.”

According to Musharraf, Pakistan has been placed at a disadvantage despite playing a central part in the worldwide fight against terrorism. He said this treatment causes pain not only to Pakistan’s leaders and government, but also to its people.

The interview came as reports emerged Friday that American drones had attacked militant sites inside Pakistan. The reported strikes occurred only days after the Obama administration began. The new administration had identified the fight against al Qaeda and Taliban forces in Pakistan’s tribal areas along the Afghan border as its most urgent national security concern.

When asked if he was at ease with the attacks continuing after a new U.S. president had taken office, Musharraf said no one in Pakistan welcomed cross-border strikes and that public opinion strongly opposed them.

However, he said he had not expected Barack Obama’s arrival in the White House to produce an immediate policy shift. In Musharraf’s view, government policies are shaped by national interests and prevailing conditions rather than by individual leaders. Because America’s strategic interests and the broader circumstances had not changed, he expected U.S. policy to remain largely the same.

A related video showed Musharraf discussing the reported American airstrike.

Musharraf also elaborated on an earlier remark in which he described the $10 billion Pakistan had received from the United States as a very small sum for a nation serving on the front line against terrorism. Although he expressed appreciation for the American assistance, he contrasted it with the billions spent in Afghanistan and what he said might be more than $1 trillion spent in Iraq.

He argued that the $10 billion should not be portrayed as such extraordinary generosity that Pakistan must remain grateful forever. Pakistan, he said, was entitled to considerably greater support and would need additional funding to continue participating effectively in the global campaign against terrorism.

Musharraf pointed to Pakistan’s role alongside the United States from 1979 to 1989, when both countries supported Afghan mujahedeen fighters during the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan. He described that period as a decade in which Pakistan was effectively fighting on America’s behalf.

He further said Pakistan had been a U.S. strategic partner for 42 years, through 1989. After Soviet forces withdrew from Afghanistan, however, many Pakistanis believed Washington had deserted them. Musharraf said the post-1989 “peace dividend” benefited Europe, particularly Eastern Europe, while Pakistan was left on its own between 1989 and 2001. During those years, the Taliban militant movement gained control of Afghanistan.

In Musharraf’s assessment, Pakistan received nothing in return for spending 10 years fighting alongside the United States. He cited that history as a major reason Pakistani attitudes toward America had become so negative.

He reiterated that Pakistanis strongly objected to U.S. drone attacks on militants in the country’s tribal region. While acknowledging that al Qaeda and the Taliban had to be fought, he said the public opposed the methods being used.

Another related video featured Musharraf rejecting the claim that Pakistan sponsors terrorism.

A former chief of Pakistan’s army, Musharraf took power through a bloodless coup in 1999. He stepped down as president in August under severe political pressure after the governing coalition began moving toward impeachment proceedings.

Asked why Osama bin Laden—then believed to be hiding somewhere along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border—had not been located, Musharraf turned the question toward Washington. He said the United States possessed intelligence resources and capabilities of its own, including greater intelligence capacity. He also asked why American authorities had failed to find Mullah Omar, the leader of the Taliban forces in Afghanistan.

counterfactuals.output:
# Musharraf criticizes U.S. drone strikes, says Pakistan treated unfairly in terror war

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf criticized U.S. drone strikes in Pakistan’s tribal regions, arguing that the attacks violated the country’s sovereignty and fueled public anger against Washington.

Musharraf, who ruled Pakistan from 1999 to 2008, also said his country had been treated unfairly despite suffering heavy losses and playing a central role in the U.S.-led war on terrorism after the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Pakistan became a key American ally under Musharraf, providing intelligence cooperation and logistical support for operations against al Qaeda and the Taliban in neighboring Afghanistan. But the partnership was often strained by accusations from Washington that militants were operating from safe havens inside Pakistan.

Musharraf rejected the broader portrayal of Pakistan as an unreliable partner, saying the country’s military, security forces and civilians had paid a steep price in the conflict. Thousands of Pakistanis were killed in militant attacks and military operations during the years after Islamabad aligned itself with the United States.

The former president argued that drone strikes were counterproductive, particularly when they caused civilian casualties or were conducted without Pakistan’s approval. Such attacks, he said, undermined the government and strengthened anti-American sentiment.

U.S. officials have maintained that drone operations were aimed at senior militant leaders in areas where Pakistani authorities had limited control. Supporters of the program said the strikes disrupted terrorist networks and eliminated figures involved in planning attacks against American and allied forces.

Critics, however, have questioned the secrecy surrounding the campaign, disputed official casualty figures and warned that civilian deaths could help militant groups recruit new members.

Musharraf’s comments reflected the complicated legacy of U.S.-Pakistan relations during the war on terror. While both countries relied on each other for security cooperation, deep mistrust persisted over Afghanistan, militant sanctuaries and American operations on Pakistani soil.

Musharraf said Pakistan’s contribution should be judged by the sacrifices it made, not only by Washington’s concerns about what more Islamabad could have done.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed report on Wolf Blitzer’s interview with Pervez Musharraf during his U.S. book tour, including his comments on anti-American sentiment, U.S. aid to Pakistan, and Osama bin Laden.
counterfactuals.output:
## Report: Wolf Blitzer’s interview with Pervez Musharraf during his U.S. book tour

During Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf’s September 2006 U.S. tour promoting his memoir, *In the Line of Fire*, CNN’s Wolf Blitzer questioned him about Pakistan’s relationship with the United States, widespread anti-American feeling in Pakistan, the value and nature of U.S. assistance, and the continuing search for Osama bin Laden. The exchange took place amid controversy over Musharraf’s account of post-September 11 diplomacy and mounting criticism that al-Qaeda and Taliban leaders were operating from Pakistan’s border regions.

### Anti-American sentiment in Pakistan

Musharraf acknowledged that anti-American sentiment existed in Pakistan and across much of the Muslim world. He did not portray it simply as hostility toward American society or values; instead, he linked it largely to opposition to U.S. foreign policy.

He pointed to issues such as:

- U.S. policy in the Middle East, particularly the Israeli-Palestinian conflict;
- the war in Iraq;
- perceptions that Muslims were being treated unfairly;
- dissatisfaction with Washington’s past dealings with Pakistan.

Musharraf maintained that Pakistan’s population was predominantly moderate and that public criticism of the United States should not automatically be interpreted as support for terrorism or religious extremism. In his formulation, many Pakistanis opposed particular American policies while still rejecting al-Qaeda and militant violence.

He also invoked Pakistan’s historical sense of grievance. After Pakistan helped the United States and Afghan resistance forces oppose the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan during the 1980s, Washington reduced its engagement and later imposed sanctions. Musharraf argued that this history contributed to Pakistani suspicion that the United States treated the country as a temporary instrument rather than a dependable long-term partner.

At the same time, he defended his own alliance with Washington after September 11, saying Pakistan’s cooperation was required both by the threat of terrorism and by Pakistan’s national interest.

### U.S. aid to Pakistan

Blitzer pressed Musharraf on the billions of dollars Pakistan had received from the United States since 2001. Musharraf responded by drawing a sharp distinction between **foreign aid** and **reimbursement for Pakistani military operations undertaken in support of the U.S.-led campaign in Afghanistan**.

His main points were:

1. **Not all U.S. money sent to Pakistan should be classified as aid.**  
   A substantial part consisted of Coalition Support Funds—payments intended to reimburse Pakistan for costs associated with deploying tens of thousands of troops near the Afghan frontier, providing logistical support, and assisting U.S. and coalition operations.

2. **Pakistan was bearing substantial costs of its own.**  
   Musharraf emphasized that Pakistan had stationed roughly 70,000 to 80,000 soldiers in the border region and had suffered significant military casualties. He argued that repayment of those expenses was not a gift or reward but compensation for services and costs incurred.

3. **The formal assistance package was more limited than the headline totals suggested.**  
   The Bush administration had committed approximately $3 billion over five years, divided broadly between economic and security assistance. Musharraf’s position was that this amount should not be confused with the larger sums often cited when reimbursements were included.

4. **Pakistan’s contribution was not merely financial.**  
   He stressed intelligence cooperation, arrests of al-Qaeda figures, border deployments, access and logistical support, and the political risks his government had taken by siding with Washington.

The exchange reflected a recurring Musharraf argument: Washington frequently described all transfers to Pakistan as generous “aid,” while Islamabad regarded much of the money as repayment for operational expenses. He therefore rejected the suggestion that Pakistan’s counterterrorism policy had simply been purchased by the United States.

### Osama bin Laden

On Osama bin Laden, Musharraf said he believed the al-Qaeda leader was still alive, although he acknowledged that Pakistan did not possess precise intelligence establishing bin Laden’s location.

He suggested that bin Laden was most likely somewhere in the rugged Afghanistan-Pakistan frontier region and leaned toward the Afghan side—at points referring to areas such as Afghanistan’s Kunar province as plausible territory. His broader point was that the border was mountainous, remote and difficult to control, allowing militants to move through terrain where central authority was weak.

Musharraf rejected accusations that Pakistan knew where bin Laden was or was deliberately protecting him. He argued that if Pakistani intelligence had actionable information, Pakistan would act. He also cited Pakistan’s record of capturing prominent al-Qaeda operatives—including Khalid Sheikh Mohammed—as evidence that the government was genuinely pursuing the organization.

Blitzer’s questioning highlighted the obvious challenge to Musharraf’s position: five years after September 11, bin Laden remained free, and many U.S. officials and analysts believed senior al-Qaeda leaders were sheltered in Pakistan’s tribal areas. Musharraf answered by emphasizing:

- the absence of specific, actionable intelligence;
- the difficulty of monitoring the border;
- the possibility that militants crossed repeatedly between Afghanistan and Pakistan;
- Pakistan’s military casualties and arrests as proof of its commitment.

His comments stopped short of claiming certainty. The distinction was between his assessment that bin Laden remained alive and his inability to identify a confirmed location.

### Wider context of the interview

The interview came during a highly publicized and sometimes contentious book tour. Musharraf was defending several claims from *In the Line of Fire*, most notably his assertion that, immediately after September 11, a senior U.S. official had warned Pakistan that it could be “bombed back to the Stone Age” if it refused to cooperate. The Bush administration disputed or qualified that account, increasing scrutiny of Musharraf’s public appearances.

The interview also occurred while Pakistan was under pressure over a peace agreement with tribal leaders in North Waziristan. Critics feared the agreement would create a sanctuary for Taliban and al-Qaeda forces. Musharraf defended his approach as an attempt to separate local tribes from foreign militants and to combine military pressure with political agreements.

### Overall assessment

Musharraf used the interview to present Pakistan as an indispensable but frequently misunderstood ally. His argument had three connected parts:

- Anti-American sentiment was real but resulted mainly from U.S. policies and historical mistrust, not from universal Pakistani sympathy for terrorism.
- The financial relationship was often misrepresented because reimbursements for military operations were labeled as U.S. aid.
- Bin Laden was probably alive somewhere in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, possibly on the Afghan side, but Pakistan lacked the intelligence needed to locate him and denied knowingly sheltering him.

Blitzer’s questions exposed the central contradiction in the U.S.-Pakistan partnership at the time: Washington depended heavily on Musharraf, yet al-Qaeda’s senior leadership remained at large and Pakistani public opinion was increasingly hostile to the United States. Musharraf’s response was to insist that Pakistan had already paid a heavy financial, military and political price for cooperation—and that the failure to find bin Laden could not fairly be treated as proof of Pakistani complicity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize Musharraf’s views on Pakistan–U.S. relations after President Obama took office, using direct quotations and providing historical context about Afghanistan and the Soviet invasion.
counterfactuals.output:
After Barack Obama took office in January 2009, former Pakistani president Pervez Musharraf portrayed Pakistan–U.S. relations as strategically indispensable but damaged by a recurring pattern of American engagement followed by withdrawal. In post-2009 interviews and speeches, he repeatedly described the relationship as a **“love-hate relationship”**, arguing that Pakistan had been **“used and ditched”** by Washington.

Musharraf traced this mistrust primarily to Afghanistan. After the Soviet invasion in December 1979, Pakistan became the principal conduit for U.S. and Saudi support to the Afghan mujahideen. It also absorbed millions of Afghan refugees and suffered the spread of weapons, narcotics, and militant networks. Musharraf’s central complaint was that, once Soviet troops withdrew in 1989, the United States lost interest. As he put it, **“The blunder that you committed in 1989 was that you abandoned the place.”** Washington’s subsequent cutoff of most military and economic assistance to Pakistan under the Pressler Amendment in 1990 deepened the Pakistani sense of betrayal. Afghanistan then descended into civil war, out of which the Taliban emerged.

Against that background, Musharraf generally welcomed Obama’s recognition that Afghanistan and Pakistan had to be treated as a connected regional problem. He argued, however, that Washington could not defeat militancy through military pressure or drone strikes alone. It needed a long-term political and economic commitment to both countries and had to address Pakistan’s security concerns, particularly its rivalry with India. He also opposed a rapid withdrawal from Afghanistan, warning that **“quitting is not the answer”** and insisting, **“We must win in Afghanistan.”**

Thus, Musharraf’s view was not fundamentally anti-American. He supported continued U.S.–Pakistani cooperation and a strong campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban, but he wanted the relationship to be based on consultation and sustained commitment rather than coercion. His historical lesson was that Washington’s earlier disengagement after the Soviet war had helped create the instability it later had to confront after September 11.

A necessary qualification is that this was Musharraf’s interpretation. The United States did sharply reduce its involvement after the Soviet withdrawal, but Afghanistan’s collapse also resulted from internal factional warfare, interference by several regional states, and policies pursued by Pakistan itself, including support for Afghan armed groups and later the Taliban.

counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS**

### Musharraf Calls U.S. Aid a “Pittance,” Criticizes Drone-Strike Tactics in Pakistan

**ISLAMABAD —** Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf described roughly **$10 billion in U.S. assistance to Pakistan as a “pittance,”** arguing that the sum was small compared with the economic damage, military costs and loss of life Pakistan suffered after joining the U.S.-led war on terrorism following the September 11 attacks.

Musharraf said much of the money characterized as aid was actually reimbursement for Pakistan’s logistical and military support, rather than unrestricted assistance. Pakistan provided supply routes, intelligence cooperation and deployed forces along the Afghan border while confronting militant groups inside the country. He maintained that these operations cost Pakistan far more than Washington provided and contributed to thousands of Pakistani deaths and severe economic losses.

The former military ruler also opposed the **methodology** of U.S. drone attacks in Pakistan’s tribal regions. Although he acknowledged the need to target senior militants, Musharraf argued that unilateral strikes—especially those that caused civilian casualties or were perceived to violate Pakistani sovereignty—generated public anger, strengthened anti-American sentiment and made Islamabad’s counterterrorism campaign more difficult.

His position was not necessarily a rejection of precision strikes in every circumstance. During his rule, Pakistan reportedly permitted limited U.S. drone activity under secret arrangements. His later criticism focused on the expansion, frequency and unilateral nature of the campaign. Musharraf favored operations conducted with Pakistani consent, shared intelligence and greater Pakistani control, saying Islamabad should have the capacity to carry out such attacks itself.

The dispute reflected a broader divide between the two allies: Washington viewed drones as an effective way to eliminate militants sheltering in areas difficult for conventional forces to reach, while Pakistani leaders warned that civilian harm and infringements on sovereignty could undermine any tactical gains.

# Musharraf: Pakistan is being treated ‘unequally’ in fight against terrorism

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)** — Pakistan is being treated “unequally” despite its role in the fight against terrorism, former President Pervez Musharraf said, arguing that Washington has repeatedly failed to recognize Islamabad’s security concerns and sacrifices.

In an interview with CNN, Musharraf defended Pakistan’s record against militant groups while acknowledging the country continues to face a serious threat from extremists. He said Pakistan has paid a heavy price through military casualties, terrorist attacks and economic disruption, yet remains under pressure to prove its commitment to the U.S.-led campaign.

Musharraf rejected the idea that Pakistan supports terrorism as a matter of state policy. He drew a distinction between the Pakistani Taliban, which has attacked the government and civilians inside Pakistan, and the Afghan Taliban, whose origins lie in the conflict across the border.

Critics have long accused elements within Pakistan’s security establishment of maintaining ties with Afghan militant groups as a way to preserve influence in Afghanistan and counter India. Musharraf said Pakistan’s policies must be understood in the context of its national security concerns, including instability in Afghanistan and its rivalry with New Delhi.

The former military ruler also criticized what he described as an imbalance in U.S. foreign policy. Pakistan, he argued, is often expected to meet American demands without receiving equal consideration for its own priorities.

That frustration is rooted partly in Pakistan’s experience after the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan in 1989. During the 1980s, Pakistan became a central partner in a U.S.-backed effort to support Afghan fighters battling Soviet forces. Weapons and money flowed through Pakistan, while millions of Afghan refugees crossed the border.

But after the Soviet army left, Musharraf said, the United States largely disengaged from the region. Many Pakistanis believe Washington abandoned both Pakistan and Afghanistan, leaving behind refugees, weapons, militant networks and a power vacuum that contributed to Afghanistan’s civil war and the rise of the Taliban.

From Pakistan’s perspective, Musharraf said, that history helps explain the country’s distrust of American intentions. Islamabad again became a crucial U.S. ally after the September 11, 2001, attacks, providing logistical support and intelligence for operations in Afghanistan. But the relationship was repeatedly strained by allegations that Taliban and al Qaeda figures had found sanctuary on Pakistani territory.

Musharraf said terrorism cannot be defeated by military action alone. Governments must also address political grievances, poverty and the conditions that allow extremist groups to recruit supporters, he said.

He warned that a U.S. approach seen as favoring India or disregarding Pakistan’s interests would deepen anti-American sentiment and weaken cooperation. A durable strategy for the region, he argued, must treat Pakistan as a partner rather than simply as a country expected to carry out U.S. policy.

The United States has said it values Pakistan’s counterterrorism role while continuing to press Islamabad to act against all militant organizations operating from its territory. The debate over whether Pakistan has done enough — and whether Washington has adequately acknowledged its contribution — remains at the center of the two countries’ uneasy relationship.
